transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. Welcome in — what brings you in to see me today?

Uh… yeah, they sent me over from the station. I’m an EMT, and I was in the bay, and the airway bags weren’t— they weren’t set right. So I kept moving them into this pattern that I knew was the right one, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud to keep it lined up.

My lieutenant kept telling me to stop, but I couldn’t just step away. It felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad. Like… you know how if one thing’s off on a rig, then everything after that is off? It was like that, but bigger. So they said I needed to come talk to someone.

When you were arranging the bags and repeating the numbers, did part of you feel that this was excessive or didn't quite make sense, or did it feel like it was genuinely necessary to prevent something bad from happening?

It felt necessary. I mean, excessive maybe to them, because they were looking at me like I was holding up the whole bay, but I knew the airway bags weren’t right. They had to be in the pattern, and the dispatch numbers—saying them out loud helped keep it lined up.

My lieutenant kept saying, “Step away,” but if I did that in the middle of it, it felt like the whole bay would go bad. Like when you miss one thing on a rig and then the rest of the call is already wrong before you even get there. So… yeah, I couldn’t stop it then.

Aside from this belief about the bags and numbers, have you noticed anything unusual lately—like hearing or seeing things others don't, or having other strong beliefs that people around you don't share?

Yeah, I mean… not seeing things, not like that. But people keep saying it’s “routine paperwork,” and it’s not just paperwork.

The injury review people, and some of the supervisors, they’ve been watching me through the station cameras. I know that sounds like— people hear “cameras” and they act like you’re making a big deal, but the cameras are there, they’re always there, pointed at the bay, the med room, the hallway by the coffee machine where everyone stands around pretending they’re not listening.

And my triage notes… they get changed. Not every word, but enough to make me look unsafe, like I missed something or wrote it wrong. Then it goes up the chain, and they say, “No, that’s just QA, that’s just review,” but I know what I put in. I’ve written thousands of those notes, I know my own charting. It’s like when somebody moves one piece of equipment and then acts like it was always there. So, yeah, that’s been going on.
How long has this been happening - the pattern-checking behavior and the belief that you're being watched and your notes altered - days, weeks, or longer?

Uh… longer than days. It’s not like it started this morning or something.

The camera stuff, the paperwork, the notes being off… I’d say about two months? Around there. And the station thing, the checking and putting things right, that’s been building in that same stretch too. It’s hard to pin it exactly because shifts blur together, you know, nights into days, and then somebody moves something and everyone says it was always that way… but yeah. About the last two months.

Over these past two months, have you also noticed changes in your mood—like feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or low energy, or on the other end, unusually elevated, energetic, or needing much less sleep?

I don’t know. I mean, “mood” is kind of a big word. Some days I’m angry because nobody’s listening, and some days I’m just worn out after shift, but that’s not the same as being… I don’t know, depressed, right?

Sleep’s been weird, but shift work does that anyway. You run calls all night and then people expect you to know what’s normal. Back when I was on days, I used to keep a better rhythm—coffee at the same time, gear check, paperwork before lunch if we had a gap—but now everything kind of bleeds together.

So… I’m not sure. I haven’t really been tracking it like that. I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed some big mood change, but I’ve been stressed. That’s what I know.

Aside from the issues with the bags, numbers, and feeling watched, have you noticed any changes in how you're managing other parts of your life—like your overall job performance, taking care of yourself day-to-day, or your relationships with friends and family?

Yeah… I mean, that part’s gotten bad. I’m not really on the ambulance anymore. They said it was temporary at first, like “take a breather, do desk duty,” but then even the desk stuff—notes, equipment checks—people started saying it wasn’t reliable. Which is funny, because half the time the equipment isn’t where it’s supposed to be anyway, and then you’re the one getting blamed for marking it wrong.

But yeah, they took me off the schedule. I’m not really working like I was.

At home… I don’t keep up with things the same. Laundry piles up, dishes, mail. I used to have a system for all that, like after my Saturday shift I’d reset everything, but now Saturdays don’t mean anything when you’re not scheduled. And friends… I mostly don’t see them. They text, sometimes, but I don’t really answer much. It just feels like too much to explain.

Have you noticed any changes in your ability to feel emotions or show interest in things you used to enjoy, or trouble keeping your thoughts organized when talking to people, separate from the beliefs about the cameras and notes?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t know if it’s “emotions” exactly, but most days I just kind of sit there. In my apartment.

There’s stuff I used to do, like cooking—real cooking, not just opening something—and I used to call the guys for basketball. We had a whole thing, same gym, and one guy always brought this terrible orange ball with no grip, I don’t know why he kept using it… anyway. I don’t call them now. I see the food in the fridge and I know it’s there, and I just… don’t start. It goes bad.

And there’s, like, trees outside the corner of the window—three of them—and I’ll just sit there looking, or not even looking really. Hours go. I’m not sad exactly. It’s more like I can’t get myself to care enough to move onto the next thing. Even simple stuff. Cooking, calling someone, anything.

This drop in motivation, pulling away from friends, and not caring about things like cooking or basketball - has that been going on for the same two months as the camera and notes concerns, or did you notice it starting earlier or later than that?

I think it’s been around the same time… maybe it’s hard to separate it, honestly. Like, I keep trying to put it in order, but the days don’t line up right in my head.

What I know is, most days now I just sit in my apartment. There are those three trees in the corner of the window—well, outside the window, but from where I sit they’re all kind of in one corner—and I’ll realize I’ve been there a long time. Food’s still in the fridge, and I meant to cook it, but I don’t. I used to actually cook, like make something with a pan and everything, not just eat crackers over the sink.

And basketball… I haven’t been calling the guys. I keep thinking I should, then I don’t. It’s not even that I decided I don’t like them. I just can’t get myself to start anything. So yeah, I guess it’s been going on with the rest of it, or close to it. I just didn’t notice it as a separate thing at first.
Have you been using any alcohol, drugs, or new medications/supplements in the past few months, or have you had any medical issues like head injury, seizures, or thyroid problems?

I don’t know… I mean, I don’t think there’s anything like that. I’m not taking some new pill or powder or whatever, if that’s what you mean.

Alcohol… not really a thing. I’ve had beers before, sure, everybody does after a shift sometimes, or used to. There was this one place near the station with these awful sticky tables—anyway, I haven’t been doing anything different like that lately.

Drugs, no. And medical stuff… I don’t think so. No one told me I had thyroid anything. Head injury—working EMS you bang your head on cabinets and doorframes, people’s stairs, all that stupid stuff, but not like… not some big thing I went to the hospital for. Seizures, I don’t think so. Would I know? I guess someone would’ve told me.

Before these last two months when the camera concerns and checking behaviors started, did you notice any smaller changes—like feeling more suspicious, socially withdrawn, or 'off' in your thinking—going back further, even 6 months or so?

Yeah… if I’m being honest, I think it goes back before the camera thing. Maybe not in the same way, but things started getting weird after I hurt my shoulder and ribs during that ambulance transfer—about eight months ago, I guess.

It was one of those transfers where everything’s cramped and somebody says “just pivot” like that solves physics, and the stretcher wheel caught, or maybe the doorway—anyway, I got twisted up pretty bad. After that, I wasn’t really myself. I kept thinking it was just pain or being off work or not sleeping right, but… yeah, that’s when it started feeling like things weren’t lining up the same. So maybe six months, eight months—around then.

But yeah, they took me off the schedule. I’m not really working like I was.

At home… I don’t keep up with things the same. Laundry piles up, dishes, mail. I used to have a system for all that, like after my Saturday shift I’d reset everything, but now Saturdays don’t mean anything when you’re not scheduled. And friends… I mostly don’t see them. target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Most days I just sit in my apartment with the tres in the corner and food still in the fridge, not calling the guys for basketball or cooking like I used to, because I can't get myself to care or start anything.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, I don’t know if it’s “emotions” exactly, but most days I just kind of sit there. In my apartment.

There’s stuff I used to do, like cooking—real cooking, not just opening something—and I used to call the guys for basketball. We had a whole thing, same gym, and one guy always brought this terrible orange ball with no grip, I don’t know why he kept using it… anyway. I don’t call them now. I see the food in the fridge and I know it’s there, and I just… don’t start. It goes bad.

And there’s, like, trees outside the corner of the window—three of them—and I’ll just sit there looking, or not even looking really. Hours go. I’m not sad exactly. It’s more like I can’t get myself to care enough to move onto the next thing. Even simple stuff. Cooking, calling someone, anything.

inference.note: Two-month duration with prominent negative symptoms (avolition, anhedonia, social withdrawal, functional decline) alongside persecutory delusions and compulsive-like ritualistic behavior driven by delusional belief supports F20.9; F22 remains possible if functional decline is solely attributable to delusions rather than true negative symptoms, though the breadth of impairment (occupational, self-care, social) and behavioral disorganization make schizophrenia more likely. No clear mood episode reported, keeping mood disorder with psychosis less likely.

doctor.question: This drop in motivation, pulling away from friends, and not caring about things like cooking or basketball - has that been going on for the same two months as the camera and notes concerns, or did you notice it starting earlier or later than that?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timing of reduced motivation, social withdrawal, and loss of interest, which directly correspond to negative symptoms.

patient.answer:
I think it’s been around the same time… maybe it’s hard to separate it, honestly. Like, I keep trying to put it in order, but the days don’t line up right in my head.

What I know is, most days now I just sit in my apartment. There are those three trees in the corner of the window—well, outside the window, but from where I sit they’re all kind of in one corner—and I’ll realize I’ve been there a long time. Food’s still in the fridge, and I meant to cook it, but I don’t. I used to actually cook, like make something with a pan and everything, not just eat crackers over the sink.

And basketball… I haven’t been calling the guys. I keep thinking I should, then I don’t. It’s not even that I decided I don’t like them. I just can’t get myself to start anything. So yeah, I guess it’s been going on with the rest of it, or close to it. I just didn’t notice it as a separate thing at first.

inference.note: The added negative symptoms (avolition, anhedonia, social withdrawal) combined with marked functional decline over the same 2-month period, alongside persecutory delusions and delusion-driven ritualistic behavior, fit the broader symptom profile of schizophrenia better than an isolated delusional disorder. F22 is now less likely since delusional disorder typically does not include prominent negative symptoms or this degree of global functional deterioration.

doctor.intent: Rule out substance use or medical conditions that could explain psychotic and negative symptoms, and assess whether the symptoms have persisted long enough to meet duration criteria
doctor.question: Have you been using any alcohol, drugs, or new medications/supplements in the past few months, or have you had any medical issues like head injury, seizures, or thyroid problems?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about substance use, medications/supplements, and medical causes such as head injury, seizures, or thyroid problems, which are not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… I mean, I don’t think there’s anything like that. I’m not taking some new pill or powder or whatever, if that’s what you mean.

Alcohol… not really a thing. I’ve had beers before, sure, everybody does after a shift sometimes, or used to. There was this one place near the station with these awful sticky tables—anyway, I haven’t been doing anything different like that lately.

Drugs, no. And medical stuff… I don’t think so. No one told me I had thyroid anything. Head injury—working EMS you bang your head on cabinets and doorframes, people’s stairs, all that stupid stuff, but not like… not some big thing I went to the hospital for. Seizures, I don’t think so. Would I know? I guess someone would’ve told me.

inference.note: Ruled out substance/medication-induced and general medical condition causes of psychosis (no drug use, no thyroid/head injury/seizure history). Symptoms of delusions (surveillance, tampered notes), disorganized/compulsive-like behavior tied to delusional beliefs, negative symptoms (avolition, anhedonia, social withdrawal, blunted affect), and functional decline persisting ~2 months without a clear mood episode remain consistent with schizophrenia spectrum illness. Mood symptoms do not meet criteria for a primary mood disorder with psychotic features, keeping F20.9 as the leading diagnosis.

patient.answer:
Yeah… if I’m being honest, I think it goes back before the camera thing. Maybe not in the same way, but things started getting weird after I hurt my shoulder and ribs during that ambulance transfer—about eight months ago, I guess.

It was one of those transfers where everything’s cramped and somebody says “just pivot” like that solves physics, and the stretcher wheel caught, or maybe the doorway—anyway, I got twisted up pretty bad. After that, I wasn’t really myself. I kept thinking it was just pain or being off work or not sleeping right, but… yeah, that’s when it started feeling like things weren’t lining up the same. So maybe six months, eight months—around then.

inference.note: Symptom duration now established at 6-8 months (exceeding the 1-month minimum for schizophrenia), with persistent delusions of persecution/surveillance and thought content changes (bags/numbers pattern), accompanied by prominent negative symptoms (avolition, anhedonia, social withdrawal, blunted affect) and functional decline across work, self-care, and relationships. No substance use, medication, or medical/neurological cause identified. Mood symptoms do not meet criteria for a primary mood episode with psychotic features, and the chronicity/negative symptom burden argues against brief psychotic disorder or schizophreniform disorder (which requires <6 months). This supports schizophrenia as the primary diagnosis.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits persistent delusions of persecution (belief that supervisors/cameras are monitoring him and altering his notes) and disorganized/compulsive-appearing behavior (rigid ritualistic arrangement of equipment tied to delusional fear) that he does not recognize as excessive, indicating fixed, non-bizarre-but-firmly-held persecutory delusions rather than true OCD with insight. These psychotic symptoms have persisted for at least 6-8 months, accompanied by prominent negative symptoms (avolition, anhedonia, social withdrawal, blunted affect, self-neglect) and clear functional decline (removed from ambulance duties, poor self-care, social isolation). No manic or depressive mood episode of sufficient duration/severity was identified to support a mood disorder with psychotic features or schizoaffective disorder, and no substance or medical etiology was found. The combination of positive (delusions) and negative (avolition, blunted affect, social withdrawal) symptoms lasting more than 6 months with functional decline meets criteria for schizophrenia; because affective and catatonic subtypes are not specified and presentation is mixed, F20.9 (unspecified) is most appropriate.
